purpose:
Broadland District
Council’s response to the Drayton Neighbourhood Plan
(2026-2040) Pre-submission Draft consultation (Reg. 14).
content:
Broadland District
Council’s response to the Drayton Neighbourhood Plan
(2026-2040) Pre-submission Draft consultation (Reg. 14).

The process of preparing a modified Drayton
Neighbourhood Plan was commenced by the Parish Council in 2025.
Following an update to the evidence base and a review of the
effectiveness and relevance of the 2016 Plan, a Neighbourhood Plan
Survey was undertaken with residents and stakeholders. This work
has led to the production of a draft, modified Neighbourhood Plan,
featuring wholesale changes to policies from the existing 2016
Plan.
 
The draft, modified Drayton Neighbourhood Plan
has been published by the steering group for pre-submission
consultation (in compliance with Regulation 14 of the Neighbourhood
Planning (General) (Amendment) Regulations 2015) between 20th July
and 31st August 2026. The target audience for this consultation is
the community of Drayton as well as a range of stakeholder bodies.
Broadland District Council is one of the stakeholders that has been
consulted on the draft Plan.
 
The proposed consultation response from the
District Council is enclosed with this form. This features comments
from officers across the Planning team, as well as from the
Community Asset  Manager.

In
general, the comments made as part of the proposed response focus
on the need for greater clarity of proposed policies within the
Neighbourhood Plan. In many cases, the comments refer to the fact
that there is duplication within the Neighbourhood Plan of policies
that are set out either within the Greater Norwich Local Plan or
within the National Planning Policy Framework 2026.
 
The
comments are intended to assist the Neighbourhood Plan steering
group in ensuring that the Neighbourhood Plan is fit for purpose
and that it meets the basic conditions for neighbourhood planning,
as set out in 
legislation. Following the
consultation, the steering group will consider all of the representations received from consultees
before preparing the final draft Neighbourhood Plan and supporting
documents for submission.
 

Broadland District Council could decline to
respond to the consultation, or certain of the comments proposed
could be withdrawn before submitting a response. However, it is
felt that each of the comments proposed suggests a way of improving
the suitability and value of the Neighbourhood Plan.

purpose:
To make minor operational
amendments to the Regulatory Enforcement Policy as required on an
on-going basis
content:
To make minor operational
amendments to the Regulatory Enforcement Policy as required on an
on-going basis

To amend the Fixed Penalty Notice (FPN) charge
matrix in Appendix 1 of the Regulatory Enforcement Policy
2026–2029 by increasing the maximum FPN from £1,000 to
£5,000. This amendment applies specifically to step 4, which
sets the scale points used to determine penalty bands. The
graduated approach to setting FPNs will remain, with penalties
based on factors such as the type and scale of waste and repeat
offending, rather than applying a £5,000 penalty to every
offence.

In March 2026, the Government published a
Waste Crime Action Plan, setting out a coordinated national
strategy to tackle waste crime. One of the key changes was an
increase to the maximum Fixed Penalty Notice (FPN) for fly-tipping
offences, from £1,000 to £5,000. This gives local
authorities the ability to issue much larger on-the-spot fines for
less serious fly-tipping cases, as an alternative to expensive
prosecutions through the courts.
 
Littering fines will also increase from a
maximum of £500 to £750.
 
Government is encouraging councils to use FPNs
more confidently where the evidence is sufficient, rather than
defaulting to warning letters or only prosecuting serious cases.
The Environmental Protection team already follows a
well-established and embedded FPN procedure for fly tipping
offences.
 
The Regulatory Enforcement Policy 2026 - 2029
details a clear decision-making procedure on when to issue an FPN
versus prosecution and introduces a sliding fee scale for FPNs
dependent upon levels of harm and culpability. The maximum fine
detailed in the policy is at the current legislative maximum level
of £1000.  In September 2026 this
will increase to £5000. 
Therefore, the Policy will require amendment.

The alternative is to leave Appendix 1 of the
Regulatory Enforcement Policy 2026–2029 unchanged, retaining
the maximum FPN of £1,000. However, this would prevent the
Council from issuing higher penalties and using the full range of
sanctions for the most harmful fly-tipping offences or those
involving the greatest culpability.

content:
To delegate to the S151 Officer,
in consultation with the leader, authority to spend funding from
the Devolution and LGR reserve.
 

To spend up to £40,000 from the Devolution and LGR
Reserve on legal advice and other fees associated with the
recent LGR decision.
 

The SNC administration opposes the LGR minded
to decision issued on 25 March 2026, and
wishes to obtain legal advice on whether this decision can be
challenged.
 
There are time limits for any challenge to be
made, and thus legal advice needs to be obtained swiftly.
 
Given this advice is specifically relating to
the LGR decision, it is appropriate to charge this to the
Devolution and LGR reserve.
 
Once legal advice is received Cabinet will
then be asked to make a decision as to
whether to proceed with formal legal action.

contrary to the SNC administrations
position, and would not allow the legal
robustness of the minded to decision to be appropriately
assessed.
 
To fund the legal advice from the normal legal
services budgets. – This work is directly linked to LGR, and
thus it is more appropriate to charge these costs to the Devolution
and LGR reserve.

purpose:
To approve
all the preliminary stages of making Neighbourhood Plans (with the
final adoption being decided by Council).
content:
To approve
all the preliminary stages of making Neighbourhood Plans (with the
final adoption being decided by Council).


Swainsthorpe
Parish Council applied to South Norfolk Council in
February 2024 to designate a Neighbourhood Area for the purpose of
producing a Neighbourhood Plan. Since that time, the Council has
supported the Neighbourhood Plan steering group in terms of
funding, professional advice and guidance from officers, and other
forms of practical support. The process of producing the Plan has
seen the steering group undertaking consultation with residents and
other stakeholder organisations, with a view to developing and
drafting Neighbourhood Plan objectives and policies. This has been
with the assistance of an independent consultant.

The proposed Neighbourhood Plan, along with
necessary supporting information, has now been submitted to South
Norfolk Council, in accordance with Regulation 15 of the
Neighbourhood Planning (General) Regulations 2012. It is now
proposed to progress the Plan through to the next stages of
consultation and independent examination.

Officers will arrange for the Neighbourhood Plan to
be published and will invite comments from the public, stakeholder
bodies and previous consultees over a minimum period of six weeks.
This requirement is set out in Regulation 16 of the Neighbourhood
Planning (General) Regulations 2012.

The Reg. 16 publication period will be followed by
an independent examination which will be carried out by a (yet to
be appointed) accredited Neighbourhood Plan examiner, in accordance
with Regulation 17.

Following the examination (which is normally dealt
with via written representations), the examiner will produce a
report recommending whether or not the
Neighbourhood Plan should proceed to a referendum (with or without
certain modifications). South Norfolk Council will then consider
this report and decide whether or not to
approve the examiner’s recommendations and whether the Plan
should proceed to a referendum.
 


On submission of a Neighbourhood Plan to the local
planning authority, the authority must undertake an assessment of
the proposed plan against certain criteria. This is required by
Part 6 of Schedule 4B of the Town and Country Planning Act
1990.

The following sets out details of the assessment
against each of the prescribed criteria:

Is the parish/town council authorised to act?

Swainsthorpe Parish Council applied to South Norfolk Council to
designate its Neighbourhood Area
following the extent of the parish boundary. This application was
approved in February 2024. It is therefore considered that the
Parish Council is authorised to act in
relation to this neighbourhood
area.

Do the proposals and
accompanying documents:
(a) Comply with the rules for submission to the Council?

Regulation 15 of the Neighbourhood Planning
Regulations 2012 (as amended) states that the submitted documents
should include:

·    
A map or statement identifying the area to which the
plan relates.

·    
A Consultation Statement, which contains details of
those consulted, how they were consulted, summarises the main
issues and concerns raised and how these have been considered and,
where relevant, addressed in the Neighbourhood Plan.

·    
The proposed Neighbourhood Plan.

·    
A Basic Conditions Statement, showing how the Plan
meets the basic conditions set out in Schedule 4B of the 1990
Act.

·    
An SEA screening assessment and, if required
as a result of the latter, an
SEA.

The Parish Council has supplied all of the above documentation.

(b) Meet the definition of a Neighbourhood
Plan?

The Swainsthorpe
Neighbourhood Plan meets the definition of a Neighbourhood Plan as
set out in Section 38A of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act
2004, containing (as it does) a series of planning policies that
seek to manage development within the parish.

(c) Meet the scope of Neighbourhood Plan
provisions?

The Neighbourhood Plan clearly states that it is a
development plan for Swainsthorpe,
which runs until 2046. The Neighbourhood Plan does not make any
provision regarding excluded development. Excluded development is
that which is either a ‘county matter’ (relating to
minerals), any operation relating to waste development, or
development consisting wholly or partly of a national
infrastructure project.

The Neighbourhood Plan only relates to the
Swainsthorpe Neighbourhood Area and it does not repeat an existing planning
permission. It is therefore considered that it satisfactorily meets
the provisions defined in Section 38B of the Planning and
Compulsory Purchase Act 2004.

Has the parish/town council undertaken the correct
procedures in relation to consultation and publicity regarding the
Neighbourhood Plan?

Regulation 14 of the Neighbourhood Planning
Regulations 2012 states that, before submitting the Neighbourhood
Plan to the local planning authority, the Qualifying Body should
publicise the Plan and consult the public and stakeholder bodies
over a period of six weeks.

The pre-submission (Reg. 14) consultation undertaken
by the Parish Council in relation to the draft Neighbourhood Plan
is summarised in the Consultation Statement. This provides details
of the publicity that was undertaken at this (and prior)
consultation stages and the bodies that were consulted on the draft
Plan. A copy of the draft Neighbourhood Plan was received by the
District Council, for comments, at this stage (which were duly
made).
 


The legislation states that the local planning
authority may only refuse to progress a submitted Neighbourhood
Plan to the next stages if it considers that any of the specific
criteria discussed above have not been met or if the Neighbourhood
Plan proposal is considered a repeat proposal, as defined in
paragraph 5 of Schedule A2 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase
Act 2004.

As stated in the previous section, it is considered
that all of the specific criteria have
been met. The Neighbourhood Plan is not a repeat proposal as
defined in legislation.
topline: The Assistant Director of Planning has decided to approve the preliminary stages of making a Neighbourhood Plan for Swainsthorpe Parish Council.

purpose:
Amendments to the Councils
Independent Policy to facilitate assistance to a wider
range of vulnerable
residents
content:
Amendments to the Councils
Independent Policy to facilitate assistance to a wider
range of vulnerable
residents

To temporarily amend for this financial
year.

·      
The Contribution Grant. The Grant that links to the DFG mandatory
means test, will be amended from up to£5,000 to up to
£20,000. For example, a requirement from an applicant of a
£25,000 contribution would be reduced to £5,000. The
Contribution Grant restriction on availability of the grant to an
applicant with £16,000 or over, in a current or savings
account, will be raised to £30,000.

·      
 Increase the Top Up grant from
£10,000 to a maximum of £20,000

·      
 Increase the Serious Illness Grant from
£5,000 to £8,000

·      
 Increase the carer support grant from
£5,000 to £8,000

·      
 Increase the maintenance grant from
£2,000 to £4,000

In 2025/26 the council will demonstrate
meeting the budget obligation to the Better Care Fund through a
combination both spend and committed funds. In previous years the
budget has been met just through spend which resulted in a
significant carry forward of committed funds
which would then become part of the following year spend. As a
result, the majority of carry forward of committed funds will not
be part of this year’s obligation to the Better Care Fund as
this
would be double counting. Therefore, without
this carry forward and a budget provision of £1,302,418 there
is an availability of funds which will allow the Council to commit
up to £1.6 million in 2026/27 as we will be able to spend
the
£1.3million budget and have a reset of
an outstanding commitment of around £300,000 that follows on
to the next financial year. Therefore, these conditions provide an
opportunity to uplift certain grants detailed in the
Council’s
independent living policy through a DP1
Portfolio Holder Decision, temporarily (for the year) to increase
delivery and availability for Broadland residents and respond to
demand in the next financial year. At the end of the year
2026/27
the financial position will be assessed, and a
policy review may be required.

None at present the Independent Living policy is comprehensive
with a
wide range of possible
assistance, no further revision is required.
topline: The Assistant Director of Individuals and Families has decided to temporarily amend the Council's Independent Living Policy to increase financial assistance for vulnerable residents.

To
transfer / spend up to £500,000 from the Devolution and LGR
Reserve to the authority(s) holding the joint
LGR transition budget to fund LGR transition costs.
 

The LGR
minded to decision issued on 25 March 2026 means that we need to
start actively preparing for 3 new unitaries to come into effect from 1st
April 2028.
 
Significant LGR implementation costs are
forecast to be incurred in the next two financial years (2026-27
and 2027-28) before vesting day, ranging between £22.3m in
the single unitary business case, £26.310m in the two unitary
business case and £33.86m in the three unitary business
case.
(Source: Draft LGR MoU).
 
A £2.7m Government Grant
(£900k per Unitary) is to be received, which will offset some
of these costs.
 
The LGR implementation costs are expected
to be shared 50% Norfolk CC, and 50%
shared equally amongst the 7 districts.
 
The share to
SNC in 2026/27 is likely to be c£500k (£7m x 7.14%). We
therefore need to be in a position to
transfer resources to the LGR budget holding authority(s) when
requested to do so.
 
Processes will be put in place to ensure
appropriate oversight of monies being spent from the LGR transition
budgets. Likely to be either via the Chief Execs group or the
Norfolk s151 Officer group.

 
 

To only
pay our contribution when specific invoices are raised to SNC -
This would be an inefficient process and not in the spirit of
collaborative working.
 
To not
contribute to LGR implementation costs. - There is an expectation
that all authorities will contribute to LGR implementation costs,
and the share to SNC (7.14%) is reasonable.
topline: The Assistant Director of Finance has decided to delegate authority to spend funding from the Devolution and LGR reserve for the creation of 3 new unitaries.

purpose:
Commuted
Sums
content:
Commuted
Sums

Allocation of commuted sums

South Norfolk Council has two affordable housing commuted
sum payments that were received in lieu of onsite provision of
affordable housing at an Orchard Homes development on Land at
Sycamore Farm, Pulham Market (Planning
Ref:2018/0598) and a large phased
development in South Wymondham (Planning Ref:
2011/0505).  Two payments were received
from South Wymondham: one from Vistry
and one from Taylor Wimpey.
Combined, the commuted sums total c£46,000; expire
between June 2026 and July 2027; and must be used for the provision
of affordable housing in South Norfolk. 
All daily accrued interest must also follow the original
capital receipt so will be added to the sum
total.
 
Approx. £20,000 from 2018/0598 expires in October
2026 and is for the “Provision of Affordable housing which
meets needs of South Norfolk”
The combined remaining balance of approx. £26,000
from Ref 2011/0505 expire in June 2026 and July 2027 and are to be
used for the “Provision of Affordable housing within the
District of South Norfolk”.  
  
Given the limited funds available also limits the appetite
of the RPs active in South Norfolk to apply for the use of the
funds despite several attempts by the Enabling team to get RPs to
engage.
Regardless, a suitable use for the funds must be found to
avoid a repayment (plus interest) back
to the original developer. 
 
The Enabling team discussed alternative suitable uses which
included offering the funds to an RP to
support tenure conversion from AHO to ART on any suitable S106
site.
The team concluded the only real viable site was the 100%
affordable housing scheme being developed by Orbit HA at
Spirketts Lane, Harleston (Planning
ref: 2023/3610)
To be known as “Harolds Gate”, this 100%
affordable home development will comprise 162 affordable homes to
include a mix of AHO and ART homes.  
 
Subject to both parties entering into a grant funding
agreement, SNC will grant fund £46,000 (+ interest) to Orbit
to deliver a 2 bed 4 person house for
affordable rent in lieu of a shared
ownership property.  The property type
and plot number has been proposed by Orbit as the one that best
meets their own internal requirements including financial viability
and marketing of the other shared ownership homes.  SNC has agreed to the proposal, subject to
receiving delegated approval to use the funds for this
purpose. 
 
 

In January 2026, a request to all
13nr RPs active in the South Norfolk district for suitable projects
to fund using the remaining 2026 and sole 2027 affordable housing
commuted sums was circulated via e-mail.
No proposals were
received. 
The Enabling team at SNC approached Orbit
with this opportunity due to a lack of other suitable projects to
fund: delivering additional homes for
affordable rent is one of the Council’s top
priorities.  This project is deliverable
within timescales and budget.
topline: The Director of Place at South Norfolk Council has decided to allocate commuted sums for affordable housing to Orbit Housing Association.

purpose:
The Norfolk Police and Crime Panel is a joint committee hosted
by Norfolk County Council. The Home Office provides a grant to host
authorities to maintain the Panel, and this allocation has remained
unchanged since its establishment in 2012.
 
The grant is now issued under a three-year agreement, reflecting
the government’s plan to end the Police and Crime
Commissioner model in 2028. At that point, governance functions
will transfer to Mayors or local council leaders, and Police and
Crime Panels will be replaced.
 
For the first time, forecast expenditure for 2025–26 is
expected to exceed the Home Office grant due to inflation and pay
awards.
 
At its meeting on 28 October 2025, the Panel considered several
savings proposals, but not all were accepted, resulting in an
anticipated overspend.
 
Norfolk Leaders have agreed in principle that their councils
will contribute towards costs above the Home Office grant for the
current three-year period. They specified that the total overall
additional contribution is to be capped at 20% of the grant
allocation and apportioned between local authorities as set out in
the Panel Arrangements. For District Councils, this would mean a
contribution resulting in a maximum of £1,286.80 over the
three-year period.
